source: Qi et al. (2025) Large Language Models Meet Symbolic Provers for Logical Reasoning Evaluation (ProverQA, ICLR 2025)
finding: On a new first-order logic set built with a symbolic prover, strong LLMs do well on easy items and fall to about half on hard items, even with chain of thought.
numbers: ProverQA 1,500 items. CoT accuracy easy/medium/hard: GPT-4o 94.2/79.4/50.0; Claude-3.5-Sonnet 95.2/83.6/56.4; Llama3.1-70B 90.4/73.2/46.8; Llama3.1-8B 75.6/46.6/33.6.
quote: barely exceed 50% accuracy on the hard subset, even with CoT prompting
limits: Synthetic, prover-checked. Older models (GPT-4o 2024-08, Claude-3.5 2024-06). Not the newest reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Long FOL proof chains are the failure zone. The agent should hand deduction to a checker, not trust prose.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Large Language Models Meet Symbolic Provers for Logical Reasoning Evaluation (ProverQA, ICLR 2025)
finding: Chain of thought helps a lot on easy or simple-rule sets but little on hard ones. The gain shrinks as difficulty grows.
numbers: Mean CoT gain over standard prompting across 7 models: ProverQA easy +12.86, medium +8.43, hard +3.86 points; ProntoQA +16.57; ProofWriter +14.36; FOLIO +5.41. Example FOLIO: GPT-4o 67.86 to 72.14.
limits: Averages over 7 models. Authors say the hard-set bottleneck is not CoT capability.
agent_relevance: More thinking text is not the fix for hard logic (supports G1/G2: use code checks).

source: Qi et al. (2025) Large Language Models Meet Symbolic Provers for Logical Reasoning Evaluation (ProverQA, ICLR 2025)
finding: Irrelevant premises and shuffled premise order both cost accuracy on first-order problems.
numbers: GPT-4o CoT hard set: 50.0 (distractors, shuffled) to 57.4 (no distractors) to 62.4 (no distractors, premises in proof order). Medium: 79.4 to 82.2 to 87.4. Easy: 94.2/94.4/95.6.
limits: One model (GPT-4o), one prompting mode.
agent_relevance: Order premises and strip irrelevant rules before an S4 consistency check.

source: Qi et al. (2025) Large Language Models Meet Symbolic Provers for Logical Reasoning Evaluation (ProverQA, ICLR 2025)
finding: Shortcut control: removing the universal rules from 60 items drops accuracy, so models are not just answering from world knowledge on this set.
numbers: N=60 items. GPT-4o direct 58.33 to 43.33; CoT 68.33 to 45.00. Llama-3.1-70B direct 65.00 to 48.33; CoT 65.00 to 53.33.
limits: Small N=60. Corrupted accuracy is still near or above chance for 3-way labels in places, so some prior-knowledge use remains possible.
agent_relevance: Use this kind of ablation to test that a pass is not fitted (G3).

source: Han et al. (2022) FOLIO: Natural Language Reasoning with First-Order Logic
finding: Expert-written natural-language reasoning set with parallel first-order formulas, checked by a prover. Fine-tuned small models and few-shot LLMs score low.
numbers: 1,430 conclusions over 487 premise sets. Test majority baseline 38.5% (87 True, 78 False, 61 Unknown). Flan-T5-large fine-tuned 65.7; Llama-13B few-shot 33.63; Llama-70B 43.97; text-davinci-002 49.53; GPT-3.5 58.34.
limits: Chance is 33%. Later papers report GPT-4 CoT about 70 (see Logic-LM line).
agent_relevance: FOLIO is the standard real-language FOL test. GPT-4-level models are only about 70 percent without a prover.

source: Han et al. (2022) FOLIO: Natural Language Reasoning with First-Order Logic
finding: Translating English to first-order formulas: syntax is usually valid but the formula often gives the wrong answer when executed.
numbers: NL-to-FOL few-shot: GPT-3.5 syntactic validity 93.3, execution accuracy 56.0; GPT-4 93.9 and 63.8. Zero-shot GPT-4 syntactic validity 86.1 but execution accuracy 51.7.
limits: The gap between valid and correct is the main finding.
agent_relevance: Valid-looking formulas are not proof of correct translation. Translation is the weak link; S4 rule checks need a source-faithful formalisation.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: Translating to logic and calling a solver beats plain and CoT prompting on most logic sets, with the largest wins where reasoning is not simple forward chaining.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy Standard / CoT / Logic-LM: PrOntoQA 77.40/98.79/83.20; ProofWriter 52.67/68.11/79.66; FOLIO 69.11/70.58/78.92. Average gain over standard 39.2 (GPT-3.5) and 24.98 (GPT-4); over CoT 18.4 (GPT-3.5) and 10.44 (GPT-4).
limits: Counter-example: on PrOntoQA GPT-4 CoT (98.79) beats Logic-LM (83.20). Gains vary by dataset.
agent_relevance: Solver beats CoT when reasoning is not simple forward chaining. Choose by problem type.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
finding: Many formalisations do not parse. A few repair rounds raise the executable rate.
numbers: Executable rate before to after self-refinement: FOLIO GPT-4 79.9 to 85.8%; GPT-3.5 66.7 to 84.3%. AR-LSAT GPT-4 32.6 to 39.8%; GPT-3.5 11.3 to 21.8%. Average +5.01 points in executable rate.
limits: Unparseable cases fall back to CoT, which mixes the two methods' results.
agent_relevance: A parse-or-fail gate with repair from the parser error matches G2 (revise from real output).

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
finding: Parse-then-prove helps small and mid models a lot but not GPT-4 on FOLIO. The GPT-4 difference is not significant.
numbers: FOLIO GPT-4: CoT 75.3 vs LINC 72.5 mean accuracy; McNemar p=0.58. StarCoder+ 15.5B: LINC 56.0 vs best baseline CoT 41.8 (+14.2). GPT-3.5: 62.6 vs 54.9. ProofWriter balanced subset (182 items): LINC 96.4 (GPT-3.5), 98.3 (GPT-4).
limits: FOLIO test 204 items. LINC uses a 10-way majority vote over translations. ProofWriter is synthetic with short sentences.
agent_relevance: The prover is not a free win. On natural text the translation step caps it.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
finding: Error types differ. The prover pipeline fails on lost information in the formula. CoT fails by stating a conclusion that contradicts its own reasoning.
numbers: Syntax errors in generated formulas: StarCoder+ 38%, GPT-3.5 24%, GPT-4 13% (commonest: one symbol used with different arities). Failure modes: L1 missing implicit facts (Person(Harry)); L2 lossy encoding (NaziGermanPolitician as one symbol); C1 CoT says no evidence then answers false.
limits: Qualitative analysis on a sample, not a count of all errors.
agent_relevance: The two methods err differently, so combining them gives a real cross-check, unlike same-model votes (G4).

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
finding: Proof depth matters. A small model with a prover stays above chance at depth; baselines fall to chance as proof depth grows.
numbers: ProofWriter: GPT-3.5 baselines above chance at depth 0 then near chance; CoT solves some depth-1 items only. StarCoder+ baselines flat near chance (1/3) at all depths; LINC well above chance, dropping with depth.
limits: Figure-level description; exact per-depth numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Deep chains need external checking.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models Using Declarative Prompting
finding: Asking the model to state constraints and letting a SAT/SMT solver plan beats asking it to write a step-by-step program.
numbers: code-davinci-002 greedy: LSAT standard 22.0, CoT 23.5, SatLM 35.0; BoardgameQA CoT 60.7 vs SatLM 79.4; ProofWriter CoT 80.1 vs SatLM 99.7; CLUTRR program-aided 58.9 vs SatLM 68.3; GSM-Sys CoT 46.5 vs SatLM 69.4. Up to 23 points over program-aided models on a hard GSM subset.
limits: On plain GSM SatLM is on par with program-aided (71.8 vs 72.7). Older model.
agent_relevance: A declarative spec plus a solver separates parsing from planning. Planning errors vanish; parsing errors remain.

source: Parmar et al. (2024) LogicBench: Towards Systematic Evaluation of Logical Reasoning Ability of LLMs
finding: A 25-rule test of propositional, first-order and non-monotonic inference: models are weakest on propositional rules, on questions whose right answer is Yes, and with negation.
numbers: Average accuracy on Yes-label items over propositional rules: ChatGPT 48.04%, GPT-4 63.98%. Models do better on No-label items than Yes-label items. Propositional harder than first-order and non-monotonic.
quote: models struggle more with inference rules of PL compared to FOL and NM
limits: Template-generated items. Three CoT prompts averaged.
agent_relevance: Per-rule error maps show which rules the base model misapplies (modus tollens, dilemmas, negation).

source: Wan et al. (2024) LogicAsker: Evaluating and Improving the Logical Reasoning Ability of Large Language Models
finding: A skill-by-skill test generator finds many failures, and feeding failed skills back as demonstrations or fine-tune data gives modest gains.
numbers: Failure rates 29% to 90% across six LLMs on 25 propositional and predicate rules (5,200 first-round cases). GPT-4o accuracy 91.92 to 97.23 after weakness-targeted examples (about +5 points); Gemini 92.06 to 96.67.
limits: Gain measured on its own weak-skill set (in-distribution). Most models better at propositional than predicate logic; fallacy recognition lowest.
agent_relevance: Targeted examples from observed failures help, within the test distribution only.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: Changing only the order of premises, which cannot change entailment, cuts accuracy sharply on modus ponens proofs.
numbers: Drop of more than 30 points in places. GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L fall 20 to 30 points; Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo fall from over 65% to under 25% (more than 40 points). Forward (proof) order best. GPT-4-turbo forward-order correct 96.5%.
quote: even in reasoning domains where the premise order does not matter, premise order does matter in LLM reasoning
limits: Modus-ponens-only logic task plus R-GSM; older models; no reasoning-tuned models.
agent_relevance: Run an entailment check under two or more orderings. Disagreement is a signal (G1).

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise Order Matters in Reasoning with Large Language Models
finding: The commonest error under bad order is inventing a fact to complete a proof step.
numbers: GPT-4-turbo error split at tau=0.5: correct 76.0%, wrong refutation 10.5%, rule hallucination 2.0%, fact hallucination 11.5%. Fact hallucination is typically the largest error type and rises as order departs from forward.
limits: 12 relevant rules, no distractors. Distractor rules magnify the effect.
agent_relevance: Verify each cited fact exists in the given premises by string match in code.

source: Saparov and He (2023) Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought (PrOntoQA)
finding: Single deduction steps are mostly valid. The weakness is proof planning: the model takes a valid but unhelpful step.
numbers: text-davinci-002, 5-hop fictional ontology: 93.2% of proof steps strictly valid, 2.4% broadly valid, 5.9% invalid; 2.4% non-atomic. Most first errors are strictly valid but misleading steps. A real-world ontology misleads less than a fictional one.
quote: quite capable of making correct individual deduction steps ... difficulty with proof planning
limits: 2022 models; synthetic ontologies. Only text-davinci-002 did well; smaller models did not.
agent_relevance: Per-step checking is cheap; search over proof branches should be done by the program.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Language models, like people, judge validity better when the conclusion is believable. Belief mixes into logic.
numbers: Tasks: natural language inference, syllogism validity, Wason selection. Models (Chinchilla, PaLM 2, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5) and humans show accuracy gains when content supports logic. Item-level human-model accuracy correlation on syllogisms t(832)=3.49, p<0.001; on NLI t(345)=4.98, p<0.001. Few-shot gives mild gains and does not remove the content effect.
limits: Older models. Only the slowest 15% of humans (over 80 s) were above chance, and only on realistic Wason rules. A bonus-payment sample did not differ.
agent_relevance: The model tends to accept wrong conclusions that sound true. Check logic with content stripped or renamed.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Human background reported in that paper: belief bias in syllogisms is large and replicated. Abstract Wason is hard even for experts.
numbers: Evans et al. cited: invalid syllogism with believable conclusion called valid about 90% of the time. Mathematics majors and academic mathematicians under 50% on the arbitrary Wason task. Longer response time is associated with accuracy (z=4.44, p<0.001).
limits: Figures are as reported in the LLM paper's review text, not re-checked against Evans 1983.
agent_relevance: Time on task and content-neutral wording are moderators; a scaffold that slows down and neutralises content should help.

source: Xu et al. (2024) Faithful Logical Reasoning via Symbolic Chain-of-Thought (SymbCoT)
finding: An all-LLM pipeline (translate to symbols, plan, solve, verify) with no external prover beats CoT and Logic-LM on average.
numbers: Gains over Naive/CoT/Logic-LM: GPT-3.5 +21.56/+6.11/+3.53; GPT-4 +22.08/+9.31/+7.88 points. Exception: FOLIO with GPT-3.5, below Logic-LM. Ablations show each module (translator, planner, solver, verifier) adds accuracy.
limits: The verifier is the same model family, so shared blind spots apply (G4). Five datasets only.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a verify step helps; but the verifier should be code or a different mechanism.

source: Lyu et al. (2023) Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Translating to a symbolic chain and solving it deterministically makes the shown reasoning the real reason for the answer, and lifts accuracy in several domains.
numbers: Beats standard CoT on 9 of 10 benchmarks; relative gains 6.3% (math word problems), 3.4% (planning), 5.5% (multi-hop QA), 21.4% (relational inference). GPT-4 and Codex reach 95.0+ on 6 of 10 datasets.
limits: Relative, not absolute, gains. One benchmark did not improve. Few-shot only.
agent_relevance: Design principle: the stated reasoning must be what computes the answer.

source: Calanzone and Teso (2024) Logically Consistent Language Models via Neuro-Symbolic Integration
finding: Large LLMs break negation and implication consistency on simple facts. A fine-tuning loss that penalises inconsistent truth assignments improves consistency, even with little data.
numbers: Reports negation, implication, reverse-implication and chained-rule consistency over BeliefBank-style sets; exact metric values not extracted this session.
limits: Fine-tuning method, not usable in a prompt-only scaffold. Numbers not read.
agent_relevance: The agent can check its own claims for negation and implication consistency in code at S4.

source: Evans, Barston and Pollard (1983) On the conflict between logic and belief in syllogistic reasoning
finding: Founding belief-bias study: people accept believable conclusions more, and the effect is strongest on invalid syllogisms.
numbers: Rates recalled from the literature, not verified here: valid-believable about 89%, valid-unbelievable about 56%, invalid-believable about 71%, invalid-unbelievable about 10%.
limits: Not opened this session. Numbers recalled; verify before use.
agent_relevance: Background only until verified.

source: Dube, Rotello and Heit (2010); Trippas, Handley and Verde (2013) belief bias as response bias
finding: Rival account: belief bias may be a shift in willingness to say valid (response bias), not a change in reasoning; cognitive ability moderates it.
numbers: None extracted. Direction recalled from memory only.
limits: Not opened this session. No numbers.
agent_relevance: If right, the fix for an agent is a calibrated decision threshold, not only more thinking.

source: SEP Classical Logic; Evans (2008) dual-process review; mental rules versus mental models debate
finding: Rival theories of human deduction (mental rules, mental models, probabilistic) agree errors rise with steps or models needed. They differ on which inferences are hard.
numbers: No numbers collected.
limits: Not opened this session. Gap marker.
agent_relevance: Do not model the agent on human errors; soundness and completeness give a stronger target.
